summary: This is an interactive SSH connection launcher that uses fuzzy finding to search through your SSH config file. It parses your SSH configuration to extract host aliases, hostnames, and comments, then presents them in a searchable menu. When you select a host, it connects via SSH, and it also supports keyboard shortcuts for additional actions like pinging or viewing configuration details.

explanations.8: This checks if the target variable is empty (the -z flag means "zero length"), and if so, the function exits early with return.
explanations.12: This creates a menu with three options (Ping, Copy-ID, Edit-Config) using fzf, which is a fuzzy finder tool that lets you search and select from a list.
explanations.14: The ssh -G command outputs the resolved SSH configuration for the target, and awk extracts just the hostname value from that output so we can ping the actual IP instead of the alias.
explanations.21: \e[1;34m sets the text color to bright blue, and \e[0m resets it back to normal; printf is being used to print colored text.
explanations.24: This reads a single keystroke from the user without requiring them to press Enter (the -k 1 -s flags).
explanations.64: This runs a Perl script that reads multiple SSH config files and processes them line by line to extract host information.
explanations.66: s/\r//g removes any carriage return characters (Windows line endings), and chomp removes the trailing newline.
explanations.70: This removes the leading # and any spaces after it from comment lines, so the comment content is preserved without the # symbol.
explanations.72: If there's already content in the buffer, it adds a separator (;;) before appending the new comment line; otherwise it just adds the comment.
explanations.78: The parentheses with $1 capture the first matched group (the Host alias name), which is then stored in the variable $new_h.
explanations.80: When a new Host is found, the previous host's data is printed, then the new host becomes the current one and the buffer is reset for its comments.
explanations.85: Similar to the Host capture above, this extracts and stores the HostName value from the SSH config.
explanations.88: The END block runs after all lines are processed, ensuring the last host entry is printed even though there's no next Host to trigger it.
explanations.94: Large padding (150 spaces) is added so that the description text (after #####) starts far to the right and doesn't overlap with the host alias display.
explanations.100: The --delimiter tells fzf to split the preview pane at the ##### marker, showing the left part (host info) in the main list and the right part (description) in a side preview.
explanations.113: The --preview runs a Perl script on field {2} (the second field, the description) to convert custom tags like <red> into actual ANSI escape codes that the terminal understands as colors.
explanations.124: Since fzf was called with --expect to capture keyboard shortcuts, its output includes the pressed key on line 1.
explanations.125: Line 2 of the fzf output contains the actual selected host line.
explanations.128: If a keyboard shortcut key was pressed (like ctrl-a or ctrl-h), call sshf_actions to handle it instead of connecting.
explanations.133: ssh -G outputs the fully resolved SSH configuration for the selected host, which we then parse to get the actual username, hostname, and key file to use.
